title: The Statue in the Square
theme: Getting to know statues, telling a picture from a statue, looking after a work of art
blurb: Ela sees a great big sparrow in the square. She calls to it, she sings to it. But the sparrow doesn't move at all! When she looks closely, she discovers the sparrow's secret all by herself.

pages.text: Ela and her grandma came to the little square. In the middle was a great big sparrow! It stood up straight on a tall stone. Ela waved: “Hello, little bird! Cheep cheep!”

nine.say: Hmm, this sparrow is very quiet…

pages.ask: Is there anything odd about this sparrow? What could it be?

pages.text: The sparrow didn't move at all. Ela called louder: “Little bird, come! I'll sing you a song!” The sparrow didn't fly. It didn't even blink. Ela felt sad. Her lips went all pouty. “Grandma, is it cross with me?”

ela.say: Little bird, come! La la la!

nine.say: Hmm… Shall we take a closer look?

predict.q: Why do you think the sparrow doesn't move?

pages.ask: Why did Ela feel sad? Do you think the sparrow is cross with her?

pages.text: Ela went closer and looked carefully. Its feathers and its eyes were made of stone! “Grandma, this sparrow is stone!” Grandma smiled: “Yes, it's a statue. An artist carved it out of stone. Tap, tap, tap!”

nine.say: Days and days of patient work.

heykel.say: Tap, tap, tap! A sparrow made of stone.

ela.say: Who made it? How many days did it take?

pages.ask: What would you like to ask the artist who made this statue?

pages.text: Just then, cheep cheep cheep! Real sparrows came. Hop, hop, they bounced. Flutter, flutter, they flapped their wings. Ela laughed: “These ones wiggle and wriggle! The statue stays still as still.” Ela counted from far away: “One, two…”

heykel.say: I'm made of stone, don't count me!

mech.done: Four real sparrows, and one stone sparrow!

pages.ask: How can you tell a real sparrow from a statue sparrow? Why do we watch from far away?

pages.text: Suddenly the wind blew, whoooo! Papers flew up and piled around the statue. Ela frowned: “Rubbish doesn't belong by a statue!” She and Grandma put the papers in the bin. Then they washed their hands.

ela.say: Rubbish doesn't belong by a statue!

mech.done: Spotless! The statue is sparkling again.
mech.msg: The papers are in the bin!

pages.ask: What can we do to keep the statues and parks in our town looking nice?

pages.text: Ela wanted to take the statue home. From her bag, Grandma took two bird pictures and two tiny stone birds. “The statue is for everyone. But you can draw it! Which ones are flat? Which can we walk around?” Pictures on the bench, stone birds by the statue!

ela.say: Can I take the little bird home?

nine.say: Flat ones on the bench, walk-around ones by the statue!

mech.done: Pictures on the bench, stone birds by the statue!

pages.ask: What things at home are flat? What things can we walk around?

pages.text: Ela sat on the bench and drew the square: statue, sun, flowers, cloud. Then she went round and round the statue, whirl, whirl! “My picture is flat. You have sides all around!” She winked at the statue: “You don't talk, but you're beautiful. Cheep cheep!”

nine.say: Your picture is flat; the statue has sides all around!

heykel.say: You don't talk, but you're beautiful. Cheep cheep!

pages.ask: If you made a statue, what would it be a statue of?

kazanim: SNAB.2 Examining a work of art — SNAB.2.ç asks questions about a work of art: Ela goes up to the statue, looks carefully and asks “Who made it? How many days did it take?”; SNAB.2.g expresses feelings and thoughts about the work: “You don't talk, but you're beautiful.”

SNAB.3 Valuing works of art and artists — makes guesses about how works are made: talks about the artist patiently carving the sparrow from stone, “tap, tap”; clears the papers away from the statue in the square and protects it.

SNAB.1.a (unverified) Tells apart art forms such as painting, sculpture and architecture — in the story, picture versus statue: on page 6 she sorts the flat bird pictures onto the bench and the tiny stone birds you can walk around next to the statue; on page 7 she says “My picture is flat. You have sides all around!” Architecture (buildings) is added as the third box in the class activity.
OB9 Art Literacy: notices a work of art in everyday life (in the square), and asks what it is and how it was made.

SDB3.2 Flexibility: Ela thinks the bird is real and changes her mind with new information; she accepts that she cannot take the statue home and turns her wish into a new activity (drawing the statue). Value: D7 Aesthetics — picks up the rubbish to protect a beautiful work.
once: Point to the sparrow on the cover: “Do you think this sparrow is real? How can we tell?” Note the answers and come back to them at the end of the story.
Show a small ornament or toy figure from home or the classroom: “What might this be made of? Who might have made it?”
sirasi: On page 1, ask “Is there anything odd about this sparrow?”; note the children's clues (it doesn't move at all, it's on a stone).

On page 2, point to Ela's pouting lips: “How is Ela feeling?” Say that it's fine to get something wrong, and that we learn new things when we look closely. Accept both answers to the prediction question; ask “Why did you think that?”
On page 3, touch the statue and copy the “tap, tap” sound together; show with your hand how the artist carved the stone.
On page 4, while counting the sparrows, point out that we watch animals from far away, and don't throw anything at them or touch them.
On page 5: we pick up litter in the street together with a grown-up, then we wash our hands. If you like, add: we don't climb on statues or draw on them.

On page 6, Ela wants to take the statue home: ask “Who does the statue in the square belong to?” In the sorting game, when the child picks an object, ask: “Can we walk around this?” Turn a flat sheet of paper and a toy figure in your hand to show the difference.
On page 7, go “whirl, whirl” around the statue together (or walk a finger around a toy); then try walking around a sheet of paper: “Does the paper have a back?”
sonra: Ela thought the sparrow was real. What made her change her mind?
What is the difference between a statue and a picture? Are the buildings in the square beautiful works that somebody made too?
What did Ela do to protect the statue? What can we do?
Put the three pictures in story order: what happened first, and what happened next?

sinif.materyal: Play dough or clay; photos of paintings, statues and buildings (2–3 of each); three boxes or baskets; an empty table (the square); paper and pastels
adim: Mix up the photos of paintings, statues and buildings. The children sort them into three boxes: “A flat painting, a statue you walk around, or a building you go inside?”
Each child makes a statue of an animal they like out of play dough; say the movements together as you do them: pinch, press, roll.
Line the statues up on the table to make a “square”. The children take turns walking around a statue and asking its artist a question.
Finally, each child draws a picture of a friend's statue; put the picture and the statue side by side and talk about the differences. Tidy the square away together.

evSoru: Why did Ela think the sparrow was cross with her?
How is a statue made? What would you make a statue out of?
How do we look after the beautiful things we see in the park or the square?

evEtk.d: On a walk, look for a statue, a beautiful building or a wall painting in your neighbourhood or town. Walk around it; let your child guess what it is made of and who might have made it. Back at home, draw what you saw together or make it out of dough. Watch birds from far away, and don't throw them bread or food.

guide.aileNotu: Today we read “The Statue in the Square.” Ela thought the stone sparrow in the square was real and called to it; when she looked closely, she worked out for herself that it was a statue carved by an artist. The children talked about examining a work of art, asking questions, telling a flat picture from a statue you can walk around, and looking after the works in our shared spaces. When you are out and about, you can look for statues and beautiful buildings together and chat about “Who made this, and how?”
